sections.COMMENTS:
The Kefallonia-Lefkada Fault marks the boundary between the NNE-directed subduction of the Hellenic Arc system to the south and the continental collision of the Hellenides belt to the north. South of Kefallonia-Lefkada, the convergence between Africa and the Aegean is thought to take place at ca. 4-5 cm/y, and GPS velocities are the fastest detected in the entire Mediterranean basin (Kahle et al., 2000; McClusky et al., 2000). North of Kefallonia-Lefkada, GPS velocities decrease rapidly and the calculated strain rates vary from more than 100-200 nanostrain/y in the Hellenic Arc to ~30 nanostrain/y in the Hellenides chain (Kahle et al., 2000; Hollenstein et al, 2003). The Kefallonia-Lefkada tectonic structure thus accommodates at least 100 nanostrain/y (Kahle et al., 1998, 2000; Hollenstein et al, 2006). GPS data indicates right-lateral relative motion across the fault of ca. 40 mm/y (Hollenstein et al, 2006), but earthquakes account for only 50% of that value (Kahle et al., 1996).
This Source is one of the most seismically active areas in the Mediterranean, characterized by earthquakes with strike-slip focal mechanisms (Papazachos et al., 1998; Vannucci et al., 2004). In 1983 an Mw 7.0 transpressive earthquake, occurred on the south-western portion of the fault (Papazachos and Papazachou, 1997; Louvari et al., 1999). The largest known seismic event in this area is the Mw 7.3 Kefallonia earthquake of 1953, which caused ca. 0.5 m of vertical displacement (Pirazzoli et al., 1994; Stiros et al., 1994). The focal mechanism reported by McKenzie (1972) for the 1953 event is a thrust and the model by Stiros et al. (1994) based on vertical displacement supports this hypothesis. However, Papazachos et al. (1994) associate this earthquake with the southern segment of the Kefallonia-Lefkada strike-slip fault, on the basis of uplift data and the distribution of seismicity.
We use the distribution of earthquakes from various authors, e.g. Papazachos et al. (2000) to constrain the depth of this source. Strike, dip and rake were based on data from various authors who analyzed the focal mechanisms (Papazachos et al., 1998; Louvari et al., 1999). We also verified that the source kinematics is consistent with the GPS velocity field and used GPS data by Cocard et al. (1999) to estimate its slip rate.

pictures.t: Seismotectonic map of the Aegean Area
pictures.c: In this map the Kefallonia-Lefkada Fault is marked as a transform fault that acts as the boundary between the Hellenic subduction to the South and the continental collision between Africa and Europe to the North (from Papadimitriou et al. [2006]).

This map clearly shows the difference between strain rates in the Hellenic Arc and strain rates in the Northern Greece offshore area, separated by the Kefallonia-Lefkada Fault (from Hollenstein et al. [2006]).
This map shows the shear strain rates associated with the Kefallonia-Lefkada Fault (from Hollenstein et al. [2006]).

pictures.t: Seismicity along the Cephalonia transform fault
pictures.c: Distribution of seismicity and focal mechanisms of the strongest events (from Louvari et al. [1999]).
The distribution of earthquakes and the analysis of the instrumental seismicity allowed to trace down the path of the fault and to determine its geometry parameters (from Louvari et al. [1999]).

pictures.t: Stress field map of the Aegean region and surroundings
pictures.c: This map shows the horizontal compression and tension axes all over the Aegean and surrounding regions. The stress axes adopted for the Southern Albania offshore source area are marked as A3 (from Papazachos et al. [1999]).
